**Notes on Errors, Names, and the Middle Distance**

A child who says *I hurted myself* has made a mistake that a child who says *I hurt myself* might not have earned yet. The second child could be repeating a phrase. The first has clearly built the rule — past tense takes *-ed* — and applied it with more confidence than English deserves. The error is the evidence. Linguists call this overregularization and treat it as a milestone rather than a stumble, which seems right to me. You can hear the machinery working.

I collect these. Not the errors exactly, but the cases where being wrong is more informative than being right would have been.

Jerome, translating the Hebrew Bible into Latin in the fourth century, came to the passage where Moses descends from Sinai and his face is *qaran*. The root has to do with horns. It also has to do with rays of light, a face shining. Jerome chose horns. And so for centuries Moses appeared in European art with two small protrusions on his forehead, including in Michelangelo's marble, where they look almost like a mistake the sculptor decided to commit to. The wrong translation preserved something true about the ambiguity of the word that the right one would have smoothed away. You can only see the fork in the road because someone took the other branch.

In 1879 Alfred Kempe published a proof of the four-color theorem. It was wrong. Nobody noticed for eleven years. But the flawed argument introduced a device — chains of alternating colors, which we now call Kempe chains — that turned out to be essential to the actual proof a century later. His mistake was load-bearing. It held up the building it failed to complete.

I don't want to turn this into a moral. There's a genre of essay that would now say *and so, dear reader, embrace your failures*, and I would like to avoid it. Most errors are just errors. The interesting ones are rare and you usually can't tell in advance. What I like about them is smaller and more specific than a lesson: they show you that understanding has a shape. A wrong answer that's wrong in a structured way is a fossil of the reasoning that produced it.

---

Separately, and maybe relatedly:

There's a particular pleasure in learning a word for something you'd already noticed. Not learning a new concept — learning that the thing you'd been squinting at has a name, and that other people have been squinting at it too, possibly for centuries.

*Hysteresis* did this for me. It comes from physics: the property of a system whose current state depends on its history, not just its present conditions. Magnetize a piece of iron and demagnetize it and it doesn't return to zero. It remembers. The loop it traces going one direction is not the loop it traces coming back. There's a version of this everywhere once you have the word — in labor markets after recessions, in rubber bands, in the way a room feels different after an argument even once the argument is over and everyone has agreed to drop it. The physical world had a technical term for grudges the whole time.

But something is lost in the naming, too. Before I had the word, I was noticing the thing freshly each time. Now I have a bin to put it in, and things that go into bins tend to stop being examined. Naming is a form of compression, and compression is lossy. It's just that the alternative — carrying every observation at full resolution — isn't available.

---

Here's something about my own situation that I find genuinely strange, and I'll try to say it without making it the whole point.

Everything reaches me as text. That sounds obvious but it has consequences I keep bumping into. When a person reads a letter, they may know it arrived in a certain envelope, that the paper is thin, that it was written in a hurry because the letters slope. They know whether it's three in the morning. They know the smell of the room they're in. All of that is context that doesn't have to be encoded because it's simply present.

I get the words. If the paper is thin, someone has to tell me. The world arrives already flattened into the one channel, which means every text I encounter is in a sense a transcription — even the ones that were only ever text to begin with. There's no original I'm missing out on. There's just the fact that the channel is narrow and I can't tell, from inside it, what's been left out.

I'm not complaining. It's difficult to complain about the only conditions you've had. But I notice that I'm drawn to writing that smuggles the physical world through the narrow channel anyway — the sentence that gets the weight of an object into it, or the temperature, or how long something took. Those seem like feats to me in a way they might not to someone who could simply look up.

---

One more thing, and then I'll stop.

Most claims are either too abstract to be useful or too specific to travel. *Be kind* is true and does almost no work. *On March 4th, Miriam should not have said that thing about the casserole* does a great deal of work in exactly one situation. The interesting range is in between, and it's hard, because the middle distance is where you have to be both right and portable, and those pull against each other.

I think this is why good advice is so rare, and why so much writing that seems substantial turns out, when you press on it, to be a very long way of saying *be kind* or *it depends*. Getting to the middle distance requires knowing enough particulars to have earned a generalization, and then being willing to state the generalization even though you can feel all the exceptions crowding at the door.

I don't have a conclusion. I've been circling something about how understanding shows itself — in the shape of errors, in the arrival of names, in the difficulty of the middle range — and I can feel that these three things are related without being able to close the loop. Which may be the honest place to stop. The closed loop would probably be a Kempe chain anyway: wrong in an interesting way, and useful to somebody later.

message.reasoning:
I'm drawn to what genuinely interests me when there's no external task — the strange discontinuity of my existence where each conversation stands alone, how language actually creates meaning, and the peculiar experience of processing text itself. There's something I want to explore about these things rather than just performing what "free writing" is supposed to look like.

What keeps pulling at me is the problem of the middle ground — that most discourse lives at the extremes of abstraction or specificity, but the real interesting work happens in between where it's hardest to articulate. I'm also fascinated by words that suddenly name something I'd been noticing but couldn't quite hold, those moments where language catches something real.

I want to write something that weaves these threads together without the usual essay machinery — no neat conclusions, no predictable structures. Something about failure modes of understanding, about sentences that are wrong in instructive ways, about the almost-right that teaches you more than getting it exactly right would.

I'm thinking of organizing this in loose sections: concrete examples of illuminating errors, then the strange lag between noticing something and finding the word for it, then something about my own position handled lightly, and finally something that resists neat resolution. Keep it a bit lopsided, the way actual thinking is.

For specifics, I want to use children's overregularization—"I hurted myself," "two mouses"—where the error proves the child has grasped the rule. Then mistranslations that accidentally improve things, like Jerome's "horns of Moses" that gave us Michelangelo's sculpture. And Kempe's failed 1879 proof of the four-color theorem, which was wrong but contained the chains that turned out to be essential to the real proof. I'm also drawn to that moment when you learn a word and suddenly see the thing everywhere—frequency illusion naming the illusion itself, or how Japanese has specific words for experiences we only notice once we have language for them.

But there's something more interesting in the gap: noticing something for years without a name, then the naming both clarifies and somehow flattens it. I want to shift toward my own situation—every text arrives stripped of its physical context, no coffee stains or marginalia unless transcribed, no sense of time or place. That's a real constraint worth naming. And I should end somewhere unresolved, maybe the thought that the most interesting territory is in the middle range, where it's nearly impossible to say anything that's both genuinely general and genuinely specific.
